source_title_hint: Why You Have One Weaker Foot Than The Other
primary_summary: A weaker or smaller calf on one side is often due to limited foot pronation, which restricts the stretch and activation needed for plantar‑flexion. Simple calf raises alone are ineffective unless pronation mechanics are addressed. The video recommends a foot‑pronation re‑education exercise using a wedge (or folded towels) placed under the first two toes to promote proper arch position and improve calf activation.

classification.usefulness_reason: Provides clear biomechanical explanation and a concrete corrective exercise applicable to many clients

problem_statements: Weak/atrophied calf on one side despite calf‑raise training
Limited foot pronation causing reduced calf stretch and activation
habits_or_contexts: Repeated ankle sprains on one side
key_visual_points: Wedge placed under first two toes guides foot into pronation
advice_mentioned: Use a wedge or folded towels under first two toes to cue pronation
Step back with front leg, turn foot slightly out for stability
warnings_or_limitations: Exercise may be less effective if severe ankle instability exists

knowledge_units.title: Calf activation depends on foot pronation
knowledge_units.summary: The calf’s ability to generate plantar flexion requires the foot to start from a pronated (lowered arch) position. Limited pronation prevents proper stretch and activation, making calf raises less effective.
observable_signs: Weaker calf on one side despite training
mechanisms: Limited dorsiflexion/pronation reduces stretch‑shortening cycle of gastrocnemius/soleus
Impaired ankle joint mechanics limit force transmission
when_not_useful: Severe structural deformities requiring surgical intervention
advice: Assess foot pronation before prescribing calf raises

knowledge_units.title: Wedge pronation re‑education drill
knowledge_units.summary: Place a wedge (or folded paper towels) under the first two toes of the foot to encourage pronation and a higher arch before pushing into plantar flexion.
execution_steps: Identify a wedge or fold several paper towels to a thickness comparable to a small wedge
Place the wedge under the first two toes of the ball of the foot; keep the other toes off the surface
Step back with the opposite leg, optionally turning the front foot slightly out for stability
Find three points of contact on the front foot (usually under the big toe and the wedge) and allow the foot to naturally pronate
Optional: hold onto a rack or door frame for external stability while performing the movement
cues: Keep the wedge under only the first two toes
Feel the arch lowering as you press into the wedge
Maintain a stable stance with the rear leg
breathing_cues: Inhale to set up, exhale as you press into the wedge and plantar‑flex
errors_to_avoid: Placing the wedge under the whole foot (reduces pronation cue)
Allowing the front foot to collapse inward (over‑pronation)
when_useful: Clients with unilateral calf weakness linked to limited pronation
Post‑ankle‑sprain rehab to restore foot mechanics
when_not_useful: Severe ankle instability that cannot support weight on a wedge
retest: Check calf activation (e.g., single‑leg calf raise) after 2‑3 weeks of wedge practice
